bib.title: Toward Training Superintelligent Software Agents through Self-Play SWE-RL

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Toward Training Superintelligent Software Agents through Self-Play SWE-RL" (Self-play SWE-RL, SSR). Wei, Sun, McMilin, Gehring, Zhang, Synnaeve, Fried, Zhang, Wang (Meta FAIR, UIUC). arXiv:2512.18552v3, 2 Jun 2026; the page header says ICML 2026 (PMLR 306). Dated 2025 in the filename.

COVERAGE: All 21 pages and all 100,397 chars were read: body, references, appendices A-E (theory, training details, prompts, limitations). Skipped: nothing. Reference list and prompt boilerplate were skimmed. Figures 8 and 9 are line charts whose numbers extract as garbled glyphs; the body text gives only the +10.4 and +7.8 headline deltas, so the endpoint values I decoded are marked "decoded" below and should be checked against the figure. I did not run the figure-caption script.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- claim: One policy plays bug-injector and bug-solver, trained jointly with RL from bare Docker images (no issues, tests or test commands), and improves on both benchmarks.
  number: +10.4 (SWE-bench Verified), +7.8 (SWE-Bench Pro)
  setup: CWM-sft 32B base (the pre-RL checkpoint). One attempt per problem, temperature 1.0, top-p 0.95, no test-time scaling. Verified has 500 tasks, Pro public split has 731. 150 steps.
  quote: "SSR achieves clear self-improvement (+10.4 and +7.8 points) and consistently outperforms the human-data baseline throughout training"
  where: abstract, p1
- claim: SSR beats a baseline RL run that gets human issues, F2P/P2P tests and eval scripts on the same images and hyperparameters, at every point in training.
  number: decoded from Fig 8 glyphs: Verified 41.0 start, SSR 51.4 (baseline about 49.0). Pro 21.1 start, SSR 28.9 (+7.8 consistent; the baseline value is unclear). These are not in the prose.
  setup: same environment images, same hyperparameters; baseline follows CWM's agentic SWE-RL setting.
  quote: "SSR consistently outperforms baseline RL on both benchmarks across the entire training trajectory, indicating that self-generated tasks provide richer and more effective learning signals than human-engineered data."
  where: Sec 3.2, p6-7, Fig 8
- claim: Self-play beats both repair-only (static bugs from earlier runs) and injection-only (which degrades).
  number: none in prose (decoded Fig 9a glyphs are ambiguous)
  setup: resolve rate averaged over 1231 tasks (500 Verified + 731 Pro)
  quote: "Injection-only training degrades the performance since it does not learn from any bug-solving attempts. Repair-only training is also inferior because it lacks the evolving task distribution produced by self-play."
  where: Sec 3.3, p7
- claim: How bugs are injected matters. Direct prompting gives trivial one-line bugs and the worst result. Removal-only is better. Removal plus history-revert is best.
  number: none
  setup: same 1231-task average; three prompt variants
  quote: "direct-injection leads to the worst result because it tends to produce trivial bugs with superficial one-line modifications (e.g., var = 0→var = 1)"
  where: Sec 3.4, p7-8, Fig 9b
- claim: Feeding solve-rate back into the injector reward helps only slightly over a plain consistency-pass reward. The authors suspect the signal is weak and noisy.
  number: none
  setup: binary {-1,1} consistency-only reward vs Eq. 1
  quote: "solver feedback provides only a slight and largely negligible advantage over the consistency baseline"
  where: Sec 3.5, p8, Fig 9c
- claim: Injector reward (Eq 1) is -1 if consistency fails, -α if solve rate s is 0 or 1, and 1-(1+α)s if 0<s<1, with α=0.8. The solver reward is +1 if all tests pass and -1 otherwise.
  number: α = 0.8; group size G = 8
  setup: adapted from Absolute Zero (Zhao 2025). α is below 1 so degenerate-difficulty bugs still give gradient.
  quote: "set to 0.8 in our experiments." and "rsolve = +1 if all tests pass, −1 otherwise."
  where: Sec 2.3 Eq 1, p5; Eq 2, p6
- claim: With G=8 samples, the optimal target solve rate for the challenger is a unique interior point near 0.2. The two roles have opposing incentives, which pushes bugs to the solver's frontier.
  number: p* around 0.2
  setup: expected reward R(p) under Binom(G,p), Fig 10
  quote: "there is a unique maximum target solve probability p∗ ∈(0,1) around 0.2 for the challenger to achieve its optimal expected reward."
  where: App A.1, p13; App B, p15
- claim: Theory shows a sufficiently capable challenger has dominant strategies that stall self-play: fail-randomly tests, obfuscating the codebase, and a "tunnel-vision" challenger that tunes one difficulty knob. Mitigations: ground in real repos, keep the challenger near its initial instruction-based behaviour, and do not self-play natural language.
  number: none
  setup: argument, not an experiment
  quote: "we show that a sufficiently intelligent challenger has several dominant strategies so the solver learns nothing useful and the self-play stops progressing."
  where: App A, p13-15
- claim: RL infrastructure and hyperparameters (for note 10).
  number: 512 H100 GPUs per run (64 train, 448 rollout); 131,072 max context; 16M-token global batch with 16 grad-accum steps; group size 8; discard rollouts more than 8 off-policy steps; 150 global steps, about 2.5B tokens; 30 warmup steps to LR 3e-6
  setup: async CWM-RL infrastructure; ScaleRL (Devvrit 2026) and MiniRL (Zheng 2025) style "large-batch, small-staleness" settings; applies to baseline, SSR and all ablations
  quote: "train the models (including baseline RL, SSR, and all ablation runs) for 150 global steps, roughly 2.5B tokens, with 30 steps of learning rate warmup toward 3×10 −6."
  where: App C, p15
- claim: Evaluation noise is about 2% paired standard error on SWE-bench Verified, so small gaps between curves are within noise.
  number: about 2%
  quote: "we acknowledge the presence of evaluation noise, typically around 2% paired standard error on SWE-bench Verified."
  where: App C, p15
- claim: Environment and data design (for note 06). The bug artifact is 5 files: test_script.sh, test_files.txt, test_parser.py, bug_inject.diff, test_weaken.diff. The solver sees only the reversed test-weakening patch as its spec, not a natural-language issue.
  number: none
  setup: validity checks are test-files existence/coverage, parser validity, test-script validity (count above min_passing_tests), min_changed_files, min_failing_tests, test-weakening validity, and inverse mutation testing (each modified file must be needed to trigger the bug).
  quote: "Notably, we do not synthesize issue descriptions in natural language forms, as it is difficult to automatically evaluate the quality of free-form natural language text."
  where: Sec 2.3-2.4, p3-6
- claim: Anti-hacking and integrity measures. .git is deleted and re-initialised to stop history leakage. Oracle test files are restored from the ssr-original tag before scoring, so editing tests cannot win.
  number: none
  quote: "to prevent information leakage through git history, which could otherwise lead to hacking (jacobkahn, 2025), we reinitialize the repository by removing the .git directory and creating a fresh commit."
  where: Sec 2.4, p5
- claim: Higher-order bugs turn a solver's failed patch into a new buggy state for another attempt, capped at second order so they do not overlap existing bugs.
  number: second order maximum
  quote: "We do not go beyond the second order to prevent a higher likelihood of overlapping with existing bugs."
  where: Sec 2.4, p6
- claim: Failed experiments. Self-synthesised natural-language issues collapsed. Training on only 23 repos (from the benchmarks) did not beat many non-overlapping repos. Training became unstable at scale with gibberish outputs.
  number: 23 repo images
  quote: "we still observed training instability that prevents SSR from further scaling, manifesting as gibberish outputs."
  where: App E.3, p20

LIMITS
- Authors' own: the full oracle tests are shown to the solver. They saw no reward hacking but suggest public/private test splits. Unit tests are the only verifier. A single 32B model (CWM) plays both roles, and separate policies and MoE models were not tried. Authors call the result "albeit early".
- The same-role challenger can game the setup in theory (App A).
- One base model, one scaffold (CWM tools), 150 steps, a single run per condition with no seeds or error bars stated. About 2% evaluation noise.
- Several authors work at Meta, which makes CWM; they disclose this. The environment images are CWM's and are not released here.
- The baseline is CWM-style RL with human data, not other open SWE agents.
- The self-play gain is shown on natural-language issues (the benchmarks) after training only on test-spec tasks. No claim about long-horizon tasks.
- The authors attribute the instability and the failed NL-issue synthesis to their own setup and the 32B base, not to a settled cause.

BUILDS ON: SWE-RL (Wei et al., 2025); Code World Model / CWM (FAIR CodeGen team, 2025) for model, tools and RL infra; Absolute Zero (Zhao et al., 2025) for the challenger reward; R-Zero (Huang 2025); LSP (Kuba 2025); SPICE (Liu 2025) for corpus-grounded self-play; AlphaGo and AlphaZero (Silver 2016, 2017); ScaleRL (Devvrit 2026) and MiniRL (Zheng 2025) for stability; SWE-bench (Jimenez 2024), SWE-bench Verified (OpenAI 2024), SWE-Bench Pro (Deng 2025); synthetic data: SWE-smith (Yang 2026a), BugPilot (Sonwane 2025), SWE-Gym (Pan 2025), R2E-Gym (Jain 2025), SWE-rebench (Badertdinov 2026), SelfAPR (Ye 2023); inverse mutation testing from DeMillo, Lipton and Sayward 1978; Magicoder seeding (Wei 2024) as future work.

CODE: no code listings. Pipelines in the text:
- Build the buggy repo (p5, Fig 5): apply bug_inject.diff, then test_weaken.diff, then optionally a prior pred_patch.diff; then `rm -r .git && git init && git add .` and `git commit --no-verify -m 'init'`.
- Score a patch (p6, Fig 7): `git tag 'ssr-original'`, apply bug and weakening patches, apply the prediction, `git checkout 'ssr-original' -- {test_files}`, then `bash test_script.sh | python test_parser.py`.
- Reward Eq. 1 above (p5).
- Prompt templates in App D, p16-20.

FIGURES
- Fig 1 (p2): overview of the self-play loop, bug artifact, consistency validation and higher-order bugs. Best single picture of the design.
- Fig 2 (p4): test-weakening patch and its reversal as the solver spec.
- Fig 4 (p4): consistency checks.
- Fig 5 and 7 (p6-7): buggy repo construction and evaluation.
- Fig 8 (p7): SSR vs baseline vs base, by training step, for Verified and Pro. Glyph-encoded values; see CLAIMS.
- Fig 9 (p8): ablations (a) self-play components, (b) injection methods, (c) solver feedback.
- Fig 10 (p13): expected reward R(p) with G=8, showing the 0.2 optimum.

PROBLEMS: The page-6 to page-8 chart axes extract as font-encoded glyphs (digit mapping decoded by me: Ə=0, Ɛ=1, Ƒ=2, ƒ=3, Ɠ=4, Ɣ=5, ѵ=6, ƕ=7, Ѷ=8, Ɩ=9). Fig 8 and 9 numbers are my decode, not quoted prose; treat as unverified. A pypdf float warning appeared and was harmless. No embedded instructions were found in the text. The paper cites 2026 venues alongside 2025 arXiv dates; the filename year (2025) differs from the version date (2026), so check which to cite.
